source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ ἔστωσαν τοὺς αὐτοὺς ἄγοντες. Τί οὖν; Ἐπεὶ οἱ πολλοί, διακρῖναι οὐ δυνάμενοι τί μὲν ὕλη τί δὲ θεὸς πόσον δὲ τὸ διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν, προσίασι τοῖς ἀπὸ τῆς ὕλης εἰδώλοις, δι᾿ ἐκείνους καὶ ἡμεῖς, οἱ διακρίνοντες καὶ χωρίζοντες τὸ ἀγένητον καὶ τὸ γενητόν, τὸ ὂν καὶ τὸ οὐκ ὄν, τὸ νοητὸν καὶ τὸ αἰσθητόν, καὶ ἑκάστῳ αὐτῶν τὸ προσῆκον ὄνομα ἀποδιδόντες, προσελευσόμεθα καὶ προσκυνήσομεν τὰ ἀγάλματα; Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ταὐτὸν ὕλη καὶ θεός, δύο ὀνόματα καθ᾿ ἑνὸς πράγματος, τοὺς λίθους καὶ τὰ ξύλα, τὸν χρυσὸν καὶ τὸν ἄργυρον οὐ νομίζοντες θεούς, ἀσεβοῦμεν. Εἰ δὲ διεστᾶσι πάμπολυ ἀπ᾿ ἀλλήλων, καὶ τοσοῦτον ὅσον τεχνίτης καὶ ἡ πρὸς τὴν τέχνην αὐτοῦ παρασκευή, τί ἐγκαλούμεθα; Ὡς γὰρ ὁ κεραμεὺς καὶ ὁ πηλός (ὕλη μὲν ὁ πηλός, τεχνίτης δὲ ὁ κεραμεύς), καὶ ὁ θεὸς δημιουργός, ὑπακούουσα δὲ αὐτῷ ἡ ὕλη πρὸς τὴν τέχνην. Ἀλλ᾿ ὡς ὁ πηλὸς καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν σκεύη γενέσθαι χωρὶς τέχνης ἀδύνατος, καὶ ἡ πανδεχὴς ὕλη ἄνευ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ διάκρισιν καὶ σχῆμα καὶ κόσμον οὐκ ἐλάμβανεν. Ὡς δὲ οὐ τὸν κέραμον προτιμότερον τοῦ ἐργασαμένου αὐτὸν ἔχομεν οὐδὲ τὰς φιάλας καὶ χρυσίδας τοῦ χαλκεύσαντος, ἀλλ᾿ εἴ τι περὶ ἐκείνας δεξιὸν κατὰ τὴν τέχνην τὸν τεχνίτην ἐπαινοῦμεν, καὶ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ τὴν ἐπὶ τοῖς σκεύεσι δόξαν καρπούμενος, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ὕλης καὶ τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς διαθέσεως τῶν κεκοσμημένων οὐχ ὕλη τὴν δόξαν καὶ τὴν τιμὴν δικαίαν ἔχει ἀλλ᾿ ὁ δημιουργὸς αὐτῆς θεός. Ὥστε, εἰ τὰ εἴδη τῆς ὕλης ἄγοιμεν θεούς, ἀναισθητεῖν τοῦ ὄντος θεοῦ δόξομεν, τὰ λυτὰ καὶ φθαρτὰ τῷ ἀϊδίῳ ἐξισοῦντες.
pass_a_gloss: But let them be the ones who hold the same views. What then? Since the many, being unable to distinguish what is matter and what is God and how much is between them, approach the idols made from matter, shall we also, who distinguish and separate the unborn and the born, the being and the non-being, the intelligible and the sensible, and give to each of them the name that belongs, approach and worship the statues? For if matter and God are the same, two names for one thing, not considering stones and woods, gold and silver to be gods, we are impious. But if they are very far apart from each other, and as much as the craftsman and the preparation for his craft, what are we accused of? For just as the potter and the clay (the clay is matter, the potter is craftsman), and God is the creator, and the matter obeys him for the craft. But just as the clay by itself is unable to become vessels without craft, and the all-receiving matter without the creator God did not receive distinction and shape and order. Just as we do not hold the clay vessel more valuable than the one who made it, nor the cups and gold ornaments more than the one who forged them, but if we praise the craftsman for something concerning them according to the craft, and he is the one who receives the glory for the vessels, and concerning the matter and the arrangement of the things that have been adorned, not the matter has the glory and the due honor, but the creator God. So, if we were to consider the forms of matter as gods, we will seem to be ignorant of the glory of the true God, equating the perishable and corruptible things with the eternal.
pass_b_english: Let the opponents keep their view. What follows? Since the multitude cannot distinguish matter from God, or define the boundary between them, they turn to idols made of matter. Must we who do distinguish and separate the unbegotten from the begotten, true being from non-being, the intelligible from the sensible, and assign to each its proper name, also draw near and worship statues? If matter and God are identical—two names for one reality—then by refusing to call stones, wood, gold, and silver gods we are impious. But if they are separated by an infinite distance, as far apart as the craftsman and the material he prepares for his art, what charge lies against us? Just as the potter is the craftsman and the clay is the matter, so God is the Creator and matter obeys Him for the work. Yet clay by itself cannot become vessels without the craftsman, and the all-receptive matter, apart from the Creator God, never received distinction, shape, and order. We do not value the ceramic above the potter, nor the cups and gold ornaments above the metalsmith; rather, when we praise the craftsman for the skill shown in them, he is the one who receives the glory for the vessels. Likewise, regarding matter and the ordering of adorned things, the glory and due honor belong not to matter but to its Creator, God. Therefore, if we treated the forms of matter as gods, we would show ourselves ignorant of the true God’s glory, equating the perishable and corruptible with the eternal.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the distinctions made in the Greek text regarding the relationship between the Creator and matter, the craftsman and his material, and the ontological categories (unborn/born, being/non-being, intelligible/sensible). Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.
